ety.text: From Middle English ynogh, from Old English ġenōg (“enough”), from Proto-Germanic *ganōgaz (“enough”) (compare Scots eneuch, West Frisian genôch, Dutch genoeg, German genug, Low German (ge)noog, Danish nok, Swedish nog, Icelandic nógur), from *ganuganą 'to suffice' (compare Old English ġeneah), or from *ga- + an unattested *nōgaz, probably ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₂eh₂nó(n)ḱe (“he has reached, attained”), perfective of *h₂neḱ- (“to reach”) (compare Old Irish tánaic (“he arrived”), Latin nancisci (“to get”), Albanian kënaq (“to please, satisfy”)).

senses.d: Used before a noun in the manner of words like some, a bit of, and so on.
ex: I've already had enough coffee today.
There is food enough for us all.
How many hired servants of my father's have bread enough and to spare!
Those pears aren't ripe enough for the children to eat (them).
You've worked enough; rest for a bit.

senses.d: Fully; quite; used after adjectives to express slight augmentation of the positive degree, and sometimes equivalent to very.
ex: He is ready enough to accept the offer.
I know you well enough; you are Signior Antonio.

senses.d: Used after certain adverbs to emphasise that a quality is notable, unexpected, etc.
ex: Talking of Mr Smith, funnily enough, I saw him just the other day.
I left my camera on the train, but luckily enough someone handed it in to lost property.

senses.d: A sufficient or adequate number, amount, etc.
ex: I have enough (of it) to keep me going.
Enough of you are here to begin the class.

senses.d: Stop! Don't do that any more! It is too much!
ex: Near-synonyms: please, cut it out, knock it off, shut up, STFU
I'm sick of you complaining! Enough!

senses.d: An instance of being sufficient, or of doing something sufficiently.

grp.label: a sufficient or adequate number, amount, etc

fr:assez.gl: to a sufficient or moderate degree; enough; sufficiently

ety.text: Inherited from Middle French assez, from Old French asez, from Late Latin ad satis, from Latin ad + satis. Cognate with Franco-Provençal asséds, Occitan assatz, Italian assai, Portuguese assaz, and Spanish asaz. Doublet of assai.
Univerbation of a + bastanza (“sufficience”), from the verb bastare (“to suffice”). Cognate with Spanish bastante.

pt:bastante.gl: many; much; a lot of; a large amount or number of

chain.g: to supply, provide, afford, give, fill, imbue, furnish, yield, produce

ety.text: Learned borrowing from Latin sufficientem, present participle of sufficiō.
From Late Latin ad satis, from Latin ad + satis; cf. French assez.
From Latin ēnormis. An assimilated form of ex- (“out of”) + norma (“rule, norm”) + -ous.

senses.d: Deviating from the norm; unusual, extraordinary.

ex: how apt wee are to receive all impressions, and chiefly the most wicked and enormous.

senses.d: Extremely large; greatly exceeding the common size, extent, etc.
ex: The enormous Jupiter is the largest planet in the Solar System.

ety.text: Inherited from Middle French enorme, borrowed from Latin ēnormis.
